gloss: The ceremony and party at which two people are married.
examples: Their *wedding* is set for the second Saturday in June.
We've been to three *weddings* this summer already.
She cried through the whole *wedding*.

gloss: The legal relationship between two people who are married.
examples: It was a long and happy *marriage*.
Both of his *marriages* ended in divorce.
They're celebrating forty years of *marriage*.

gloss: An agreement between two people to get married, and the period before the wedding.
examples: They announced their *engagement* over Thanksgiving dinner.
It was a short *engagement* — six weeks from the proposal to the wedding.
Long *engagements* are less common than they used to be.

gloss: A woman who stands with the bride during a wedding and helps her prepare for it.
examples: She asked her sister to be a *bridesmaid*.
All six *bridesmaids* wore navy blue.
Being a *bridesmaid* turned out to be more work than I expected.

gloss: The man who is getting married on his wedding day.
examples: The *groom* looked nervous at the altar.
The bride and *groom* cut the cake together.
Traditionally the *groom* doesn't see the dress beforehand.

gloss: A man who stands with the groom during a wedding.
examples: He was a *groomsman* at his roommate's wedding.
The *groomsmen* rented matching gray suits.
One *groomsman* forgot the rings in the hotel room.
contrast: Irregular plural: *groomsman* → *groomsmen*, like *man* → *men*. Both endings sound the same, /mən/.

gloss: A person who has recently gotten married.
examples: The *newlyweds* left for Hawaii the next morning.
As a *newlywed*, she was still getting used to her new last name.
The hotel gave the *newlyweds* a free upgrade.

gloss: A serious promise, especially one made publicly at a wedding.
examples: They wrote their own *vows* instead of using the traditional ones.
He broke his *vow* to quit smoking.
The couple renewed their *vows* on their tenth anniversary.

gloss: A person who shows guests to their seats at a wedding, theater, or church.
examples: An *usher* walked my grandmother down the aisle to her seat.
The *ushers* handed out programs at the door.
Ask the *usher* where section C is.

gloss: The person who leads a wedding or other ceremony and makes it official.
examples: Their *officiant* was a friend who got ordained online.
The *officiant* asked everyone to be seated.
You'll need to give the marriage license to the *officiant*.

gloss: A practice run of a ceremony or performance before the real thing.
examples: The wedding *rehearsal* is Friday at five.
We had three *rehearsals* before opening night.
The *rehearsal* dinner is at the Italian place downtown.

gloss: A list of gifts a couple has asked for, kept at a store or website.
examples: Their *registry* is at Target if you want to send something.
We picked the towels off the *registry*.
Most couples set up two or three *registries*.

gloss: A wedding held secretly or with almost no guests, often away from home.
examples: Their *elopement* shocked both families.
After pricing out a big reception, they opted for an *elopement*.
Small *elopements* in the mountains have gotten popular.

gloss: The legal ending of a marriage.
examples: Her parents' *divorce* was final last spring.
He's been through two *divorces*.
They're getting a *divorce* after eleven years.

gloss: A small arrangement of flowers worn on the wrist or pinned to a dress at a formal event.
examples: He bought her a white *corsage* for the prom.
The mothers of the bride and groom both wore *corsages*.
Her *corsage* was starting to wilt by the last dance.
contrast: The -sage ending is /ʒ/, like the middle of *measure* — kor-SAHZH, not kor-SAJ.

gloss: A large room used for formal dances and big events.
examples: The reception is in the hotel *ballroom*.
Both *ballrooms* were booked that weekend.
They cleared the *ballroom* floor for dancing at nine.

gloss: A social event where people gather to eat, drink, talk, and enjoy themselves.
examples: We're having a *party* Saturday night — you should come.
His birthday *parties* were legendary in the neighborhood.
The *party* went on until two in the morning.

gloss: An occasion or event held to mark something happy or important.
examples: The whole town turned out for the *celebration*.
There were *celebrations* in the streets after the win.
Dinner turned into a *celebration* when she announced the promotion.

gloss: A large formal party, usually held to raise money for a cause.
examples: The museum's annual *gala* raised half a million dollars.
She wore a floor-length gown to the *gala*.
Charity *galas* fill the calendar every fall.
contrast: Americans normally say GAY-luh, not GAH-luh.

gloss: A large formal party with dancing.
examples: The charity *ball* is black tie.
She's been to two *balls* this season.
The governor's inaugural *ball* was held downtown.

gloss: A big, lively party.
examples: They threw a huge *bash* for his fiftieth.
The company *bash* is at a rented warehouse this year.
Their New Year's *bashes* are the stuff of legend.

gloss: A noisy, informal party, often with music and dancing.
examples: The neighbors are throwing some kind of *shindig* tonight.
It was a real *shindig* — a band, a bonfire, the works.
Their backyard *shindigs* draw half the block.

gloss: A social event where people come to dance.
examples: There's a *dance* at the school gym on Friday.
She went to every *dance* her senior year.
The fire department holds a *dance* every spring.

gloss: A party where guests wear masks and costumes.
examples: The Halloween *masquerade* is at the old opera house.
Guests at the *masquerade* didn't take off their masks until midnight.
She's been to *masquerades* in Venice and New Orleans.

gloss: A Hawaiian outdoor feast with roast pork, music, and dancing.
examples: The resort puts on a *luau* every Thursday night.
We went to a *luau* on the beach at sunset.
Tourist *luaus* are pricey but fun.

gloss: A lively public celebration, especially in Spanish-speaking communities.
examples: The city's spring *fiesta* fills ten blocks downtown.
There was music and dancing all week during the *fiesta*.
Local *fiestas* draw crowds from three counties.

gloss: A party held to celebrate moving into a new home.
examples: We're having a *housewarming* once the boxes are unpacked.
She brought a plant as a *housewarming* gift.
They've thrown two *housewarmings* in three years.

gloss: A meal or party where every guest brings a dish to share.
examples: The office *potluck* is Wednesday — sign up for a dish.
I always bring my mom's casserole to *potlucks*.
It's a *potluck*, so nobody has to cook for thirty people.

gloss: An outdoor party where food is grilled and eaten.
examples: We're doing a *cookout* in the backyard on the Fourth.
There were three *cookouts* on our street that weekend.
Bring a folding chair to the *cookout*.

gloss: A party held in a stadium parking lot before a game, with food cooked out of car trunks.
examples: The *tailgate* starts four hours before kickoff.
Their *tailgates* have grills, a tent, and a TV.
We got to the *tailgate* early to save a spot.

gloss: A party at which children stay overnight at a friend's house.
examples: She's at a *sleepover* at Emma's tonight.
Four girls came for the birthday *sleepover*.
*Sleepovers* mean nobody gets any sleep.

gloss: An arranged time for two young children to play together, set up by their parents.
examples: We set up a *playdate* with the boy from her class.
Our kids have *playdates* every Tuesday afternoon.
The *playdate* ended in tears over a toy truck.

gloss: A small, informal social gathering of friends or family.
examples: It's just a little *get-together*, nothing fancy.
We have family *get-togethers* twice a year.
The *get-together* was moved inside because of the rain.

gloss: A group of people who have come together in one place for a shared purpose.
examples: It was a quiet *gathering* of close friends.
Large *gatherings* were banned that spring.
A small *gathering* formed on the courthouse steps.

gloss: An informal gathering of people who share an interest, usually arranged online.
examples: There's a photography *meetup* downtown on Thursdays.
He's organized dozens of coding *meetups*.
The *meetup* is at a coffee shop on Third Street.

gloss: A relaxed get-together, or the place where a group regularly spends time.
examples: It's a casual *hangout*, not a real party.
That diner was our *hangout* all through high school.
The park is one of their usual *hangouts*.

gloss: A gathering of people who have not seen each other for a long time.
examples: Our twentieth high school *reunion* is in October.
The family *reunion* draws about sixty people.
They've held *reunions* at the same lake since 1978.

gloss: An annual fall celebration at an American school or college, with a football game, a parade, and a dance.
examples: She's on the *homecoming* court this year.
The *homecoming* game drew the biggest crowd of the season.
Alumni come back for *homecoming* every October.

gloss: A formal lunch held for a group, often with speeches.
examples: The awards *luncheon* starts at noon.
She spoke at two *luncheons* last month.
The *luncheon* is thirty dollars a plate.

gloss: A large formal dinner for many people, usually to honor someone or mark an occasion.
examples: The team's end-of-season *banquet* is at the Hilton.
He's given speeches at plenty of these *banquets*.
The *banquet* hall seats four hundred.

gloss: A traveling show with rides, games, and food stands, or a public festival with costumes and parades.
examples: The *carnival* sets up in the mall parking lot every June.
She won a stuffed bear at the *carnival*.
Small-town *carnivals* still run the same rides they did decades ago.

gloss: A public event with exhibits, competitions, food, and entertainment.
examples: We go to the state *fair* every August.
Her pie won a blue ribbon at the county *fair*.
Craft *fairs* pop up all over town before the holidays.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *fare* (the price of a ride). Both are /fɛr/.

gloss: A sale of donated or handmade goods held to raise money, or an open market.
examples: The church holds a holiday *bazaar* the first weekend of December.
She bought a knitted scarf at the school *bazaar*.
*Bazaars* like that raise a surprising amount for the food bank.
contrast: Nearly identical in sound to *bizarre* (strange): buh-ZAR vs. bih-ZAR. Different words entirely.

gloss: A traveling show with acrobats, clowns, and performing acts.
examples: The *circus* is in town for three nights.
He ran off and joined the *circus* at nineteen.
Traveling *circuses* aren't what they were fifty years ago.

gloss: The activities and events that make up a celebration.
examples: The *festivities* kick off with a parade at ten.
Rain cut the *festivities* short.
She missed most of the *festivity* because of a late flight.

gloss: A smaller party held right after a bigger event ends.
examples: There's an *afterparty* at a bar down the block.
The *afterparties* usually run later than the show itself.
Only about twenty people made it to the *afterparty*.

gloss: A woman who invites and takes care of guests at an event.
examples: Bring the *hostess* a bottle of wine.
She's a wonderful *hostess* — nobody's glass stayed empty.
The *hostesses* greeted everyone at the door.

gloss: A person who is present at an event or meeting.
examples: Every *attendee* got a name tag at the door.
There were over four hundred *attendees* this year.
One *attendee* asked a question nobody could answer.

gloss: A person who takes an active part in an event or activity.
examples: Each *participant* gets a T-shirt and a race number.
*Participants* should arrive by eight.
She was a *participant*, not just a spectator.

gloss: A written or spoken request asking someone to come to an event.
examples: The *invitation* said seven o'clock, dinner to follow.
We mailed out a hundred and twenty *invitations*.
Thanks for the *invitation* — we'd love to come.

gloss: An invitation (informal).
examples: Did you get an *invite* to the party?
She sent the *invites* out by text.
I never got an *invite*, so I stayed home.
contrast: Stress moves with the part of speech: the noun is IN-vyt, the verb *to invite* is in-VYT.

gloss: The place where an event is held.
examples: We're still looking at *venues* for the reception.
The *venue* holds about three hundred people.
They changed the *venue* two weeks before the show.

gloss: The seats at an event, or the arrangement of who sits where.
examples: *Seating* is first come, first served.
We spent an entire evening on the *seating* chart.
There's outdoor *seating* for another fifty guests.

gloss: The business of providing food and drink for an event.
examples: *Catering* was the biggest line item in the budget.
They do *catering* for weddings and corporate parties.
The *catering* ran out of chicken before the last table was served.

gloss: A person or company hired to supply food and drink at an event.
examples: We booked the *caterer* six months out.
Three *caterers* gave us quotes.
The *caterer* set up two buffet lines.

gloss: Light food and drink served at an event.
examples: *Refreshments* will be served in the lobby afterward.
There's a table of *refreshments* by the window.
He stepped out for a *refreshment* between speakers.

gloss: The subject or style that an event's decorations and costumes follow.
examples: The party has a 1920s *theme*.
Her birthday *themes* have gotten more elaborate every year.
Pick a *theme* and the decorations get a lot easier.

gloss: Music, shows, or activities provided to amuse people at an event.
examples: The *entertainment* for the evening is a jazz trio.
They hired a magician for *entertainment*.
Half the budget went to food and the other half to *entertainment*.

gloss: A person who sings, acts, dances, or otherwise entertains an audience.
examples: The *performers* stayed backstage until eight.
She's a natural *performer* — the crowd loved her.
Street *performers* line the boardwalk all summer.

gloss: The person who introduces the speakers or acts at an event and keeps it moving.
examples: The *emcee* cracked a few jokes before the awards.
They needed an *emcee* for the fundraiser.
Both *emcees* wore tuxedos.

gloss: A book that visitors to an event sign, often leaving a short message.
examples: Please sign the *guestbook* on your way in.
The *guestbook* sat on a small table by the door.
They keep the wedding *guestbooks* from both ceremonies.

gloss: A folded piece of stiff paper with a printed message, sent to mark an occasion.
examples: Don't forget to sign the birthday *card*.
She still has every *card* he ever sent her.
We got about forty holiday *cards* this year.

gloss: A small gift given to each guest at a party or wedding.
examples: The party *favors* were little bags of candy.
Each guest took a *favor* from the table on the way out.
We're making the wedding *favors* ourselves.
contrast: American spelling *favor*; British English writes *favour*. Same pronunciation.

gloss: Something given to someone to mark an occasion.
examples: The *gifts* piled up on the table by the door.
It's a small *gift*, but I hope you like it.
She opened her *gifts* after the cake.

gloss: A small object kept to remember a person or an occasion.
examples: She saved a pressed flower from the bouquet as a *keepsake*.
The box was full of *keepsakes* from their travels.
He gave each grandchild a *keepsake* from the house.

gloss: A thin rubber bag filled with air or gas, used as a decoration at parties.
examples: The kids tied *balloons* to the mailbox.
One *balloon* popped and made the baby cry.
We ordered a dozen helium *balloons* for the party.

gloss: A long, narrow strip of colored paper hung up as a party decoration.
examples: They taped orange and black *streamers* across the doorway.
A *streamer* had come loose and was hanging over the punch bowl.
*Streamers* and balloons took about an hour to put up.

gloss: Small bits of colored paper thrown into the air at celebrations.
examples: *Confetti* rained down when the clock hit midnight.
We were finding *confetti* in the carpet for weeks.
The guests threw *confetti* as the couple came out.
contrast: Uncountable in English despite the Italian plural ending: *the confetti was everywhere*, never *confettis*.

gloss: A long strip of cloth or paper with a message on it, hung up at an event.
examples: A *banner* over the stage read WELCOME HOME.
They hung *banners* along the parade route.
The *banner* came loose in the wind.

gloss: A decoration placed in the middle of a table at a formal meal.
examples: Each *centerpiece* was a low bowl of white roses.
Guests were told to take the *centerpieces* home.
The *centerpiece* was so tall nobody could see across the table.
contrast: American spelling *centerpiece*; British English writes *centrepiece*.

gloss: A rope of flowers or greenery hung up or worn as decoration.
examples: A pine *garland* ran along the stair railing.
They draped *garlands* over every doorway.
The *garland* smelled like cedar all through December.

gloss: A hanging paper figure filled with candy that children hit with a stick until it breaks open.
examples: The kids lined up to swing at the *piñata*.
We filled the *piñata* with chocolate and little toys.
They sell *piñatas* shaped like every cartoon character you can think of.
contrast: The ñ is pronounced like the ny in *canyon*: pin-YAH-tuh, not pin-AH-tuh.

gloss: A bunch of hanging threads tied at one end, worn on a graduation cap or used as trim.
examples: Move your *tassel* to the left side after they call your name.
The graduates threw their caps, *tassels* and all.
Her *tassel* kept swinging into her face.

gloss: A device that explodes in the sky with colored light and noise at a celebration.
examples: The *fireworks* start at dusk down by the river.
We watched the *fireworks* from the roof.
A single *firework* went off early and startled everyone.
contrast: Almost always plural in American speech: people say *the fireworks*, rarely *a firework*.

gloss: A small paper tube that makes a loud bang when it explodes.
examples: Someone set off a *firecracker* in the alley.
*Firecrackers* are illegal in this county.
The dog hides under the bed whenever she hears a *firecracker*.

gloss: A thin stick that burns slowly with bright sparks, held in the hand at celebrations.
examples: The guests held *sparklers* as the couple left.
Give each kid one *sparkler* and stand back.
The *sparkler* burned out before I could get a picture.

gloss: A large outdoor fire built for a celebration or gathering.
examples: They built a *bonfire* on the beach after the game.
We sat around the *bonfire* until it burned down to coals.
Homecoming week always ends with a *bonfire*.

gloss: A short loud burst of trumpet music, or the noisy attention around an event.
examples: A *fanfare* announced the arrival of the guest of honor.
The building opened with a lot of *fanfare* and a ribbon cutting.
The old theater closed quietly, without *fanfare*.

gloss: A loud shout of approval or encouragement from a crowd.
examples: A *cheer* went up when the doors finally opened.
You could hear the *cheers* three blocks away.
The announcement was met with a *cheer* from the back of the room.

gloss: Words or a phrase repeated over and over by a crowd.
examples: The *chant* started in one corner and spread through the stadium.
Marchers kept up the same *chants* for two miles.
You could barely make out the words of the *chant*.

gloss: Long, enthusiastic clapping from an audience.
examples: She got a standing *ovation* that lasted four minutes.
The band came back for an encore after two *ovations*.
The *ovation* died down only when the lights came up.

gloss: A decorated platform on wheels that is driven in a parade.
examples: The senior class built a *float* out of chicken wire and tissue paper.
Twelve *floats* rolled down Main Street.
Kids on the *float* threw candy to the crowd.

gloss: A public procession of people, bands, and vehicles moving through the streets to celebrate something.
examples: The *parade* starts at nine on Fifth Avenue.
We stood on the corner and watched the *parade* go by.
The town holds two *parades* a year.

gloss: A line of people or vehicles moving forward together in a formal or solemn way.
examples: The funeral *procession* stretched for half a mile.
A candlelit *procession* wound through the square.
Both *processions* met in front of the church.

gloss: An organized walk by a large group of people to show support for something.
examples: Thousands joined the *march* on Saturday morning.
There have been three *marches* downtown this month.
The *march* ended with speeches on the capitol steps.

gloss: A public performance of music.
examples: The *concert* sold out in about ten minutes.
We've been to four of their *concerts*.
There's a free *concert* in the park every Sunday in July.

gloss: A performance or movie showing held in the afternoon.
examples: We caught the two o'clock *matinee*.
*Matinee* tickets are five dollars cheaper.
The Sunday *matinee* is usually packed with families.

gloss: An occasion when a movie is shown to an audience.
examples: There's a *screening* of the documentary at seven.
The festival added two more *screenings* after the first sold out.
The director spoke after the *screening*.

gloss: A large public exhibition where companies show their products.
examples: The auto *expo* takes over the whole convention center.
She hands out samples at three or four *expos* a year.
Admission to the *expo* is free on Sunday.

gloss: A public sale where things go to whoever offers the most money.
examples: The silent *auction* raised nine thousand dollars.
He buys most of his tools at farm *auctions*.
The painting sold at *auction* for far more than expected.

gloss: An event held to collect money for a cause or organization.
examples: The band is holding a car wash *fundraiser* Saturday.
They put on two *fundraisers* a year for the animal shelter.
The *fundraiser* brought in more than they expected.

gloss: A way of raising money in which people buy numbered tickets and one is drawn to win a prize.
examples: I bought five tickets for the *raffle*.
The *raffle* prize was a weekend at a cabin.
They run *raffles* at every home game.

gloss: A long television broadcast that asks viewers to call in and donate money.
examples: The *telethon* ran for eighteen straight hours.
Those *telethons* used to be a Labor Day tradition.
Volunteers answered phones during the *telethon*.

gloss: An event in which people compete to win a prize.
examples: She won the pie-eating *contest* two years running.
The station runs *contests* all week long.
It wasn't much of a *contest* — he led from the start.
contrast: Stress moves with the part of speech: the noun is KAHN-test, the verb *to contest* is kuhn-TEST.

gloss: A competition in which players or teams play a series of games until one wins.
examples: The chess *tournament* runs all weekend.
They've won three *tournaments* this season.
He got knocked out in the first round of the *tournament*.
contrast: First syllable is TUR-, not TOOR- or tour-: TUR-nuh-muhnt.

gloss: A public show or competition, especially one judging beauty and talent.
examples: She competed in her first *pageant* at sixteen.
The church puts on a Christmas *pageant* every year.
Small-town *pageants* still crown a queen at the fair.
contrast: The -ea- is short: PAJ-uhnt, not PAY-juhnt.

gloss: A prize or honor given to someone for an achievement.
examples: He picked up an *award* for best teacher.
The *awards* are handed out at the end of the banquet.
Her film won three *awards* at the festival.

gloss: Something given to the winner of a contest or game.
examples: First *prize* is a hundred dollars and a trophy.
There are *prizes* for every age group.
She took home the grand *prize*.

gloss: A metal cup or figure given as a prize for winning.
examples: The *trophy* sits on the mantel next to his photo.
There's a whole case of *trophies* in the school lobby.
They lifted the *trophy* at center court.

gloss: A flat piece of metal on a ribbon, given as an award.
examples: She won a gold *medal* in the two hundred meters.
His *medals* are in a drawer somewhere.
Every finisher gets a *medal* at the end of the race.
contrast: In American speech *medal*, *meddle*, *metal*, and *mettle* all sound alike — the t and d both become a quick flap.

gloss: An extra performance given after the main show, in response to applause.
examples: They played two songs as an *encore*.
The crowd stayed on its feet until the *encore*.
Most bands plan their *encores* in advance.
contrast: Borrowed from French: the first syllable is AHN, not EN.

gloss: The person an event or award is meant to honor.
examples: The *honoree* sat at the head table.
This year's *honorees* were all volunteers.
They kept the party a secret from the *honoree*.
contrast: The h is silent, as in *honor* and *hour*: ah-nuh-REE.

gloss: A person or team that reaches the last round of a competition.
examples: She was one of five *finalists* for the scholarship.
The three *finalists* performed again on Friday.
Being a *finalist* alone was a big deal for him.

gloss: The occasion of a baby coming into the world.
examples: They celebrated the *birth* of their first grandchild.
There were four *births* at the hospital that night.
He was there for the *birth* of both his kids.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *berth* (a bed on a ship or a docking space). Both are /bɜːrθ/.

gloss: The process of giving birth to a baby.
examples: She took a class on *childbirth* in her seventh month.
His great-grandmother died in *childbirth*.
Natural *childbirth* was what they'd planned on.

gloss: A ceremony at which a baby is baptized and given a name.
examples: The *christening* is on Sunday after the late service.
She wore the same gown to her *christening* that her mother wore.
There were two *christenings* that morning.
contrast: The t is silent: KRISS-uh-ning, not KRIST-uh-ning.

gloss: The ceremony at which a crown is placed on a new king or queen.
examples: Millions watched the *coronation* on television.
The *coronation* took place in the abbey.
There have been only a handful of *coronations* in the last century.

gloss: An event marking the start of something new, such as a product or a book.
examples: The book *launch* is at the bookstore on Tenth.
They've done three product *launches* this year.
Half the office came to the *launch*.

gloss: An event celebrating the first day a business, show, or exhibit is open to the public.
examples: The gallery *opening* is Thursday from six to nine.
We went to the *opening* of the new restaurant downtown.
Gallery *openings* usually mean free wine and cheese.

gloss: A ceremony held to mark the start of construction, at which the first shovel of dirt is turned.
examples: The *groundbreaking* for the new library is next Tuesday.
The mayor spoke at the *groundbreaking*.
There have been two *groundbreakings* on that block this year.

gloss: A ceremony at which a cover is removed from a statue, plaque, or new product for the first time.
examples: The *unveiling* of the memorial drew a large crowd.
There was applause at the *unveiling*.
The company staggers its *unveilings* across the year.

gloss: A person's or thing's first public appearance.
examples: She made her stage *debut* at nineteen.
The album *debut* was set for the fall.
Both *debuts* got good reviews.
contrast: The t is silent, from French: day-BYOO, not day-BUTT.

gloss: An event that presents someone's or something's best work to an audience.
examples: The spring *showcase* gives every student ten minutes on stage.
The festival is a *showcase* for new directors.
They hold two *showcases* a year for local bands.

gloss: A ceremony that makes someone a full member of a group.
examples: The fraternity's *initiation* takes place in the fall.
*Initiations* on campus are much more closely watched now.
He wouldn't say a word about the *initiation*.

ru: торжественное введение (в должность, в зал славы)
gloss: A formal ceremony admitting someone to an office, an organization, or a hall of fame.
examples: His *induction* into the Hall of Fame is in July.
The *induction* ceremony lasted two hours.
There were six *inductions* that evening.

gloss: An act or occasion of saying goodbye to someone who is leaving.
examples: They threw a *farewell* for her last day at the office.
It was a quiet *farewell* at the airport gate.
Long *farewells* always make him uncomfortable.

gloss: A show of good wishes for someone who is leaving or starting something new.
examples: The whole team gave him a great *send-off*.
She got a proper *send-off* on her last day.
The *send-offs* for the graduating class run all week.

gloss: The greeting or reception someone gets when they arrive.
examples: The troops came home to a hero's *welcome*.
She gave us a warm *welcome* at the door.
New students get a *welcome* from the dean on the first day.

gloss: Words or an action used to welcome someone or mark an occasion.
examples: He gave me a quick *greeting* and moved on to the next guest.
The card carried *greetings* from the whole family.
A handshake is the standard *greeting* here.

gloss: A public statement telling people about something that has happened or will happen.
examples: They made the *announcement* at dinner: they're expecting.
The wedding *announcement* ran in the local paper.
There were a few *announcements* before the ceremony started.

gloss: An official public announcement, often read aloud at a ceremony.
examples: The mayor read a *proclamation* declaring it Founders Day.
The city issues several such *proclamations* every year.
A framed copy of the *proclamation* hangs in the lobby.

gloss: Something said or done to show respect and admiration for someone.
examples: The concert was a *tribute* to her late husband.
*Tributes* poured in from all over the state.
He paid *tribute* to the volunteers in his speech.

gloss: An act or display that shows respect or honor for someone.
examples: The evening was a *salute* to local firefighters.
A twenty-one-gun *salute* closed the ceremony.
There were *salutes* to the graduating seniors between innings.

gloss: A ceremony or event held to remember an important person or occasion.
examples: The town held a *commemoration* of the flood's fiftieth year.
*Commemorations* were held in a dozen cities.
A short *commemoration* was added to the program.

gloss: The act of remembering and honoring someone who has died.
examples: The candles were lit in *remembrance* of the victims.
The bench was placed there in *remembrance* of her father.
A moment of *remembrance* opened the ceremony.

gloss: The act or ceremony of placing a dead body in the ground.
examples: The *burial* took place the following morning.
Only family came to the *burial*.
Records of hundreds of *burials* are kept at the church.
contrast: The vowel is the same as in *berry*, even though it's spelled with u: BAIR-ee-uhl, from *bury* (BAIR-ee).

gloss: The burning of a dead body to ashes instead of burying it.
examples: He'd asked for *cremation* rather than a burial.
*Cremations* now outnumber burials in most states.
The *cremation* was followed by a small memorial service.

gloss: A long box in which a dead body is buried.
examples: The *casket* was closed during the service.
They chose a simple pine *casket*.
Six men carried the *casket* down the church steps.
contrast: *Casket* is the usual American word; British English says *coffin*.

gloss: A box in which a dead body is buried or cremated.
examples: The *coffin* was lowered into the grave.
Rows of plain wooden *coffins* stood in the yard.
They draped a flag over the *coffin*.

gloss: A container that holds the ashes of a person who has been cremated.
examples: The *urn* sits on the shelf above the fireplace.
They picked out a simple brass *urn*.
Two *urns* were buried side by side.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *earn* (to be paid). Both are /ɜːrn/.

gloss: One of the people who carry the casket at a funeral.
examples: His three sons served as *pallbearers*.
She asked me to be a *pallbearer*.
The *pallbearers* waited by the hearse.

gloss: A person who attends a funeral or grieves for someone who has died.
examples: About two hundred *mourners* filled the church.
One *mourner* laid a single rose on the casket.
The *mourners* walked slowly to the graveside.

gloss: Deep sadness felt and shown after someone dies.
examples: The family is still in *mourning*.
She wore black for a year of *mourning*.
The flags were lowered as a sign of *mourning*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *morning* (the early part of the day). Both are /ˈmɔːrnɪŋ/.

gloss: A speech praising someone who has just died.
examples: His daughter gave the *eulogy*.
There were three short *eulogies* instead of one long one.
She couldn't get through the *eulogy* without stopping.

gloss: An expression of sympathy to someone whose family member or friend has died.
examples: Please accept my *condolences*.
Cards and *condolences* arrived all week.
He offered a quiet word of *condolence* at the door.

gloss: A gathering held before or after a funeral where people remember the person who died.
examples: The *wake* is at the funeral home from four to eight.
Half the town came to the *wake*.
Irish *wakes* in his family went on all night.

gloss: A hole in the ground where a dead body is buried, and the spot marking it.
examples: She visits his *grave* every spring.
Rows of *graves* stretched over the hillside.
There were fresh flowers on the *grave*.

gloss: A piece of ground where people are buried, usually next to a church.
examples: The old *graveyard* behind the chapel dates to 1790.
We cut through the *graveyard* on the way to school.
There are two *graveyards* on that road.

gloss: A stone marking a grave, carved with the dead person's name.
examples: The *gravestone* had worn smooth over two centuries.
Some of the *gravestones* were leaning badly.
They ordered a granite *gravestone* in the spring.

gloss: The upright stone placed at the head of a grave.
examples: The *headstone* won't be set until the ground settles.
Someone had left pebbles on top of the *headstone*.
Most of the *headstones* face east.

gloss: A stone slab that marks a grave and carries an inscription.
examples: The *tombstone* just gave a name and two dates.
Kids used to make rubbings of the old *tombstones*.
Ivy had grown up over half the *tombstone*.
contrast: The b in *tomb* is silent, and the vowel is long: TOOM-stohn.

gloss: The words carved on a gravestone in memory of the person buried there.
examples: His *epitaph* was a single line from a poem.
She read the *epitaphs* on every stone in the row.
They argued for weeks about the *epitaph*.

gloss: A stone building that holds the bodies or ashes of the dead.
examples: The family *mausoleum* stands at the top of the hill.
Marble *mausoleums* line the oldest section of the cemetery.
The *mausoleum* is locked except on visiting days.
contrast: Plural is usually *mausoleums* in American English; the Latin *mausolea* is rare and formal.

gloss: An underground room, usually beneath a church, where people are buried.
examples: The bishops are buried in the *crypt*.
Stairs led down to the *crypt* below the altar.
The cathedral's *crypts* are open to visitors.

gloss: A cloth used to wrap a dead body for burial.
examples: The body was wrapped in a plain linen *shroud*.
Green burials use a simple *shroud* instead of a casket.
The museum displayed two ancient *shrouds*.

gloss: A person whose job is to prepare the dead for burial and arrange funerals.
examples: The *undertaker* met the family at the door.
His grandfather was the town *undertaker* for forty years.
Two *undertakers* handled all the arrangements.

gloss: A person trained to prepare bodies and run a funeral home.
examples: The *mortician* walked them through the options.
She trained as a *mortician* after nursing school.
Local *morticians* met to discuss the new rules.

gloss: The state of having lost someone close to you through death.
examples: The company gives three days of *bereavement* leave.
He took time off for *bereavement* after his mother died.
*Bereavement* affects people in very different ways.

gloss: A time before a funeral when people come to see the body and pay their respects.
examples: The *viewing* is Thursday evening at the funeral home.
They held two *viewings*, one in the afternoon and one at night.
A long line formed outside the *viewing*.

gloss: A way of doing something that a group of people has followed for a long time.
examples: Throwing rice at the couple is an old *custom*.
Wedding *customs* differ a lot from region to region.
It's the *custom* here to bring food to a grieving family.

gloss: A belief or practice passed down within a family or community over many years.
examples: Pancakes on the first snow day is a family *tradition*.
The school has kept the same *traditions* since the 1920s.
It started as a joke and turned into a *tradition*.

gloss: The keeping of a custom or holiday, or a ceremony held to mark one.
examples: The town holds a quiet *observance* every November.
Religious *observances* fill the calendar that month.
The *observance* lasted about twenty minutes.

gloss: A trip away from ordinary life for a group to rest, plan, or study together.
examples: The company sends managers on a *retreat* each January.
She's been on two silent *retreats* in the mountains.
The *retreat* runs from Friday night through Sunday lunch.

gloss: A place and program where children stay for part of the summer to do activities together.
examples: He goes to *camp* in Maine for three weeks every July.
There are soccer *camps* and music *camps* all summer.
She met her best friend at *camp*.
